section.title: Haman's Downfall
section.sectionRationale: At the second banquet the trap finally springs. When the king renews his open-handed offer, Esther at last names her petition: her own life and the life of her people, sold out to destruction. Pressed to say who would dare such a thing, she points to Haman. The king storms out in fury; Haman, pleading for his life, falls across Esther's couch just as the king returns, sealing his doom. Harbonah mentions the gallows Haman built for Mordecai, and Haman is hanged on it. The plotter dies by his own device.
section.thesis: A brave queen speaks, a proud enemy is unmasked, and the gallows built for the righteous receives the wicked instead, the hidden God turning the plot back on the plotter's own head.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Esther's petition and the naming of the enemy; the king's fury and Haman's desperate plea; and the reversal by which Haman hangs on his own gallows.

verses.text: So the king and Haman went to dine with Esther the queen,

and as they drank their wine on that second day, the king asked once more, “Queen Esther, what is your petition? It will be given to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be fulfilled.”
Queen Esther replied, “If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it pleases the king, grant me my life as my {{sheelah|petition}}, and the lives of my people as my request.

For my people and I have been sold out to destruction, death, and annihilation. If we had merely been sold as menservants and maidservants, I would have remained silent, because no such distress would justify burdening the king.”
Then King Xerxes spoke up and asked Queen Esther, “Who is this, and where is the one who would devise such a scheme?”
Esther replied, “The adversary and enemy is this wicked man, Haman!” And Haman stood in terror before the king and queen.

units.label: The king's fury and Haman's plea
units.note: the proud man begging for his life

verses.text: In his {{chemah|fury}}, the king arose from drinking his wine and went to the palace garden, while Haman stayed behind to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he realized that the king was planning a terrible fate for him.

Just as the king returned from the palace garden to the banquet hall, Haman was falling on the couch where Esther was reclining. The king exclaimed, “Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?” As soon as the words had left the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face.

units.label: Hanged on his own gallows
units.note: the plot returns on the plotter

verses.text: Then Harbonah, one of the eunuchs attending the king, said: “There is a gallows fifty cubits high at Haman’s house. He had it built for Mordecai, who gave the report that saved the king.” “Hang him on it!” declared the king.
So they hanged Haman on the {{ets|gallows}} he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the fury of the king subsided.

sheelah.gloss: A petition, a request, the thing asked for. Esther has been invited three times to name her sheelah, and now she does: not treasure or rank, but life itself, her own and her people's. The word frames the whole scene as an appeal for mercy to the only earthly power who can grant it, and the reader senses a greater petition being answered behind the throne.

chemah.gloss: Burning anger, hot wrath, fury. The same royal chemah that once fell on Vashti now blazes against Haman and finally subsides only when he is dead. In a book where God is never named, the king's uncontrollable rage becomes, without anyone intending it, the instrument that removes the enemy of God's people.

ets.gloss: A tree, wood, timber; here the wooden gallows or stake Haman raised for Mordecai. The word ties the ending back to the beginning of Haman's rage: the very ets he built to display his triumph becomes the place of his death. Scripture repeatedly warns that the one who digs a pit falls into it, and here the pattern is exact.

basic.context: This is the chapter where the trap Esther has been setting finally closes. At the second banquet the king again asks what she wants, offering half the kingdom. This time she speaks plainly: someone has plotted to destroy her and her whole people. When the king demands to know who, she names Haman, sitting right there at the table. The king storms out in a rage; Haman, terrified, throws himself on Esther's couch to beg for his life, and the king walks back in to find him there. That seals it. A servant points out the gallows Haman built for Mordecai, and the king orders Haman hanged on it.
basic.hermeneutics: The central question is: who is really running this scene? There is no miracle, only a courageous queen, a hot-tempered king, and a proud man's panic. Yet the outcome is exact justice, the enemy destroyed by the very device he built. The key questions are why Esther waited until now to speak, and whether Haman's death on his own gallows is simply irony or something more. The lesson is that the God who is never named still turns the schemes of the wicked back on their own heads.
basic.originalLanguages: Esther finally names her sheelah, her petition, and it is not for wealth but for life, her own and her people's. The king's chemah, his burning fury, the same rage that once removed Vashti, now falls on Haman and only cools when he is dead. And Haman hangs on the ets, the wooden gallows he built for Mordecai. Three plain words carry the reversal: a plea for life, a royal fury, a gallows turned back on its maker.
basic.typology: Haman, the accuser of God's people who is destroyed on the very wood he prepared for the righteous, is a dark foreshadowing by contrast. The accuser is thrown down, and the one marked for the gallows is spared, a pattern fulfilled when Christ disarmed the accuser at the cross. The wood raised to kill the innocent becomes the place of the enemy's defeat.
basic.christ: Haman is the accuser and enemy who is cast down, and Mordecai the condemned man who is spared. This points forward to the cross, where the true Accuser, Satan, was defeated, and where the innocent One took the place of death so that the guilty might live. The gallows that ruined Haman anticipates the tree on which our enemy was finally overthrown.
basic.god: God is not named once in this chapter, yet His fingerprints are everywhere: the timing of the banquet, the king's rage, the servant who just happens to know about the gallows. The wicked man falls into the pit he dug for the righteous. The book is teaching us that a hidden God governs even the fury of kings to protect His people and to bring justice on their enemies.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 7 says the wicked falls into the hole he has made. Proverbs 26 warns that whoever digs a pit will fall into it. Psalm 37 promises that the sword of the wicked will pierce their own heart. And Colossians 2 shows Christ disarming the accuser and triumphing over him at the cross.
basic.oneStory: The enemy who plotted the death of God's people is destroyed on his own gallows, and the condemned man is spared. It is the gospel shape in miniature, the accuser cast down and the marked one delivered, fulfilled when Christ overthrew the true accuser at the cross and turned an instrument of death into the place of victory.

context.literary:
Esther 7 is the shortest chapter of the book's climax and the most tightly written. It has ten verses, three speakers and three movements, and every line is turned toward the last. The king asks, exclaims and commands, Esther speaks twice, and Haman does not speak at all. He is the man who has talked his way through every earlier scene, and here he stands silent while others decide his fate. His only act is to fall.

The chapter is a deliberate answer to chapter 3, and the echoes are exact. There Haman offered silver so that the Jews could be destroyed, Esther 3:9, and the decree spoke of destroying, killing and annihilating them, Esther 3:13. Here Esther says that she and her people have been sold 'to destruction, death, and annihilation', verse 4, and she uses the very three verbs of the decree. She speaks the enemy's own words back to the king and, by that, quietly identifies the source. She is also careful in what she claims. She says that had they been sold as slaves she would have kept silent, and that speaks of her sense of proportion. She argues the case as the king would see it.

The book's frame is also completed. In chapter 1 the king's anger burned against Vashti, and in chapter 2 it subsided, Esther 1:12 and 2:1. Here it burns against Haman and subsides again, verse 10, and the pair of matching phrases closes a circle. The chapter is full of movement toward and away, as the king goes out into the garden and comes back, and the whole story of Haman is decided in the time it takes to walk out and back. A careful reader will notice the brief sentence that carries the reversal: 'As soon as the words had left the king's mouth, they covered Haman's face', verse 8.
context.historical:
The chapter takes place at the second banquet, in the queen's own hall, with wine served after the meal in the Persian way. Persian nobles reclined on couches at feasts, which explains the couch in verse 8, and the whole scene depends on that detail. To fall upon the queen's couch while the king was in the palace was, in the eyes of the court, a violation of the royal household, and the king's exclamation in verse 8 would have seemed a natural charge. In a court where the queen's rooms were guarded by eunuchs and even the king's servants could not approach, the offence would have looked grave.

The method of execution matters too. English says Haman was 'hanged', and the Hebrew verb agrees, but the practice in Persian royal justice was frequently impalement on a stake. Royal inscriptions and Greek historians describe rebels being impaled, and a fifty cubit post, about twenty two metres, was built to be seen from far off. Whether Haman was hanged or impaled, the point is that the display he designed for Mordecai was used on him. The book reports the fate of his ten sons in the same terms, Esther 9:13 and 14, so the family that built its hopes on public honour ended on public display.

Harbonah, the eunuch who names the gallows, is probably the same man named among the seven eunuchs of Esther 1:10. He served at Vashti's dismissal and now serves at Haman's. The court officials who once enforced Haman's rise are now the ones who point out his end. In Persian politics, a fallen favourite quickly lost his friends. After Haman's death, his property goes to Esther, Esther 8:1, and Mordecai receives the signet ring, Esther 8:2. That is how the empire's power moves.
context.canonical:
The chapter is a full narrative version of a theme in Israel's wisdom and worship. The Psalms describe the wicked digging a pit and falling into it, Psalm 7:15 and 16, Psalm 9:15 and 16, and Psalm 57:6, and Proverbs adds that the wicked 'fall by their own wickedness', Proverbs 11:5, and that a righteous person is delivered while the wicked man 'goes in' his place, Proverbs 11:8. Psalm 37:14 and 15 describes the wicked drawing the sword against the upright, and says their swords will pierce their own hearts. Esther 7 shows what the psalms promise.

Haman the Agagite belongs to the long conflict with Amalek. The LORD swore to blot out Amalek's memory, Exodus 17:14 to 16, and Israel was told never to forget it, Deuteronomy 25:17 to 19. Saul was sent to finish the task and spared Agag, 1 Samuel 15:8 and 9, and Samuel completed it, 1 Samuel 15:32 and 33. Esther 7 is the last recorded episode of the story. Mordecai, a Benjamite of the line of Kish as Saul's father was, Esther 2:5, finishes what Saul left undone, and it is done by the hand of the LORD's providence, not by a battlefield.

The promise to Abraham stands behind all this: 'I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you', Genesis 12:3. Haman cursed the Jews and was cursed. The New Testament takes up the language of accusation and vindication. Paul asks 'Who will bring any charge against God's elect?' and answers that it is God who justifies and Christ who intercedes, Romans 8:33 and 34. Revelation says the accuser of the brothers has been thrown down, Revelation 12:10. In each of these, the accuser is silenced by a greater advocate, as Haman was silenced in front of the queen.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author's aim is to convince a threatened people that the threat has already been answered, even before it seems so. The decree of chapter 3 could not be undone by the king's own law, and yet this chapter shows the man behind it destroyed in the space of a single meal. The readers, who remember that day of dread, are meant to feel a release that carries into their own life: the powers that seem invincible are not.

He also wants them to admire Esther's manner. She does not shout. She asks for her life first, and for her people second, and she makes her case in the king's own terms, as a matter of cost to the court. When pressed, she names the man, but she names him plainly and only when asked. The author holds her up as a model of bold speech that is also careful speech.

And he writes for readers who would need to understand justice. The gallows does not come from the Jews' revenge but from the fact that a wicked plan comes back on the planner. He wants his readers to see judgment as coming from a source above themselves, so that they will wait for it and not take it into their own hands, and so that they may hold together the truth that God is just and that they are safe.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter reports Haman's death and the king's fury. It does not command anyone to seek the downfall of enemies, and it does not say that every persecutor will die in this way. The victory recorded is a particular act of deliverance for a particular people at a particular time, and it should not be read as a promise that every wicked plan will be punished in a single evening.

What the chapter prescribes by example is honest, courageous speech before authority. Esther speaks for her own life and for others, and she names a wrong when asked to. It also invites believers to trust God with justice. Proverbs warns 'Do not gloat when your enemy falls', Proverbs 24:17, and Paul tells believers to leave room for God's wrath, Romans 12:19. The story's tone of relief is legitimate, but it is not a licence for triumph. Jesus taught His people to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them, Matthew 5:44, and the reader should hold that alongside the story's satisfaction.

debates.question: Was Haman hanged or impaled?

views.label: Hanged on a gallows
views.case: The Hebrew verb is the ordinary one for hanging, and the Old Testament uses the same verb for the execution of the two eunuchs in Esther 2:23 and for the exposure of a body on a tree in Deuteronomy 21:22. The book presents a tall wooden structure, and many translations therefore say 'gallows'.

views.label: Impaled on a stake
views.case: Others point out that impalement was the usual Persian punishment for rebels, attested in royal inscriptions and by Greek writers, and that a tall stake fits the fifty cubit height. On this reading the Hebrew verb describes the display of a body on a post, and 'hanged' is an English convenience.

debates.bearing: The question does not change the point of the story. The wood built for Mordecai is used on Haman, and Paul's later use of the phrase 'hung on a tree' in Galatians 3:13 rests on the wider biblical idea of a body displayed on wood.

debates.question: What did the king think he saw when Haman fell on the couch?

views.label: He judged it an attack on the queen
views.case: The king's words, 'Would he actually assault the queen while I am in the palace?', treat it as a violation. On this view the king is looking for a reason to condemn Haman, and finds one that no one could excuse.

views.label: He knew it was a plea but used the moment
views.case: Some suggest that the king would have known Haman was pleading for his life and that the accusation is a pretext. The king had already decided, and the exclamation gives legal cover for the sentence.

debates.bearing: The narrator lets the accusation stand as the king's own reading. The irony is that Haman, who wanted to destroy the queen's people, is condemned for a movement that was only fear.

debates.question: How should believers read the satisfaction of Haman's fall?

views.label: As legitimate joy in God's justice
views.case: Scripture allows the righteous to rejoice when God vindicates them, Psalm 58:10 and 11, and to see in judgment a sign that there is a God who judges the earth. The Jews of Susa were spared a real massacre, and their relief is not a moral failing.

views.label: As a story that must be read alongside mercy
views.case: Others insist that the Bible also says that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 33:11, and that His people are told not to gloat, Proverbs 24:17. On this reading the story records justice without commending delight in it, and the fuller Christian answer is prayer for enemies.

debates.bearing: Both are biblical, and they are held together in Jesus, who prayed 'Father, forgive them', Luke 23:34. The chapter gives relief, and the rest of Scripture keeps it from turning into cruelty.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the words the study has already marked, several details in the Hebrew of this chapter are worth noticing.

Esther asks for 'my life', nafshi, which is the ordinary word for soul or self, and puts it first, before her people. It is a word that covers the whole person. She could have said 'my request' in the abstract, but she names herself, and her identity as a Jew, which she has hidden since chapter 2, is given away in the same breath. In one sentence, the secret is broken, and the reader sees why the earlier chapters made so much of the concealment.

The triplet 'destroy, kill and annihilate' in verse 4 is nearly a quotation of the decree in Esther 3:13. It is the language of the plan, and Esther turns it round to be the language of the accusation. She adds one new verb, 'sold', which recalls the money that Haman offered in Esther 3:9. The Jews were to be a purchase, a commodity bought by silver. The word carries an ironic weight for the later reader, who knows that God's people are also 'bought', though at a different price, 1 Corinthians 6:20.

The next phrase is famously difficult. Esther says the distress would not justify 'burdening the king', or, as some render it, the adversary would not be worth the king's loss. The Hebrew is compressed, and translators differ on whether she means that slavery would not have warranted troubling the king, or that the enemy could not make up the king's loss. Either way she says that this is no small matter. Her word for enemy in verse 6 is tsar and oyev, 'adversary and enemy', two words that stack, and she gives the name after the king asks who and where, as though she had let him name the crime before she named the man.

The last words are a small but telling detail. The king's rage 'subsided', a verb that Genesis uses of the floodwaters going down, Genesis 8:1. Here it is a royal fury going down, and the same verb closed the story of Vashti, Esther 2:1. The word for the covering of Haman's face, from the root for covering, is the one used earlier of his head in grief, Esther 6:12. He began the day with his head covered and ends with his face covered. The Hebrew repeats the image and lets the reader close the loop.

typology.type: Haman the adversary silenced before the throne
typology.fulfillment: The one whom Esther calls 'adversary and enemy' stands accused before the king and has no answer. He resembles the accuser of God's people, who stood at Joshua's right hand in Zechariah's vision and was rebuked, Zechariah 3:1 and 2, and who at last is 'thrown down', Revelation 12:10. The escalation is that the real accuser is silenced not by a clever queen but by the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 12:11. The type falls short because Haman was a human enemy who could be killed, while the accuser is a spiritual power finally overcome by Christ's cross and destined for the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10.

typology.type: Esther pleading, 'grant me my life and the lives of my people'
typology.fulfillment: Esther identifies herself with those under sentence and pleads for their lives as her own. It foreshadows the One who is 'not ashamed to call them brothers', Hebrews 2:11, and who shared their flesh and blood in order to free them from the fear of death, Hebrews 2:14 and 15. The escalation is that Christ does not simply plead for the condemned but takes the sentence on Himself, 1 Peter 3:18. The type falls short because Esther's plea could only ask a king for mercy, while Christ Himself bears what the law required.

typology.type: The gallows turned on the man who built it
typology.fulfillment: The device meant to destroy the righteous kills the plotter, an image of the cross where the powers thought to end the Righteous One and instead were disarmed, Colossians 2:15. The escalation is that Haman was hanged for his own guilt, while Christ was hung as the innocent in place of the guilty, Galatians 3:13. It echoes a truth about the enemy's methods: the works of darkness are turned against it, and it is the 'prince of this world' who is cast out, John 12:31. The type falls short in that Haman's death solves an immediate crisis, while Christ's answers sin and death forever.

typology.type: The people who were sold, and their rescue
typology.fulfillment: Esther says her people were 'sold' for destruction, and the story ends with them saved, free and honoured. It anticipates the promise 'You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed', Isaiah 52:3, fulfilled when believers were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ', 1 Peter 1:18 and 19. The escalation is that the redemption is not only from a decree but from sin, and the price is not silver but blood. The type falls short because the Jews of Susa were spared without any ransom being paid on their behalf, while the cost of our rescue fell on Christ.

study.christ:
Esther 7 does not point to the Messiah by name, but it draws the outlines of the accusation, the advocate and the reversal in a way that the New Testament fills in.

The chapter shows an accused people with an advocate. Esther stands before the throne and identifies herself with those under sentence: 'grant me my life as my petition, and the lives of my people as my request.' Hebrews tells of a greater identification. Jesus 'is not ashamed to call them brothers', Hebrews 2:11, and since the children share flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy the devil and free those who were held in slavery by the fear of death, Hebrews 2:14 and 15. Esther pleads that her people not be killed, and she does it at the risk of her own life. Christ pleads by giving His own. Paul asks, 'Who is there to condemn us?', and answers, 'Christ Jesus, who died, and more than that was raised to life, is at the right hand of God, and He is interceding for us', Romans 8:34.

The chapter also shows the enemy as an accuser silenced. The word Esther chooses for Haman, adversary, is the noun that in other places names those who stand against God's people. The New Testament calls the devil the accuser of the brothers, who accuses them day and night before God, and says he has been thrown down, Revelation 12:10. What ends the accusation is not human cleverness. It is the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 12:11. On the cross, God cancelled the written debt that stood against us and disarmed the powers, Colossians 2:14 and 15. Like Haman, the accuser is undone by the very instrument he used.

The third link is the wood. The tall gallows was prepared for a righteous man, and it became the instrument of the unrighteous man's death. On another day, a tree was prepared for the Righteous One. Peter says that God raised Jesus 'whom you had killed by hanging Him on a tree', Acts 5:30, and Paul says Christ became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. Where Haman died on his own gallows for his own sin, Christ died on ours for our sin. That is the point at which the resemblance turns into a contrast, and where the gospel is heard most clearly. He is the innocent one on the wood, so that the guilty may be spared.

The caution is the usual one. Esther is not the Messiah, and Haman's death is not the last judgment. The parallels are those of pattern, and no detail of the banquet is a code. But a Christian reader who watches the accuser fall and the advocate stand hears, under the story, the larger news that no charge can stand against the people of God, because God Himself has justified them.
study.god:
Esther 7 shows a God who stands behind a book that does not name Him, and the character of that God can be traced.

He is just. The gallows falls on the man who built it, and no human hand arranged that. The Psalms say that 'the LORD is known by the justice He brings; the wicked are ensnared by the work of their hands', Psalm 9:16, and that the one who plots harm meets it, Psalm 7:15 and 16. Nothing in the chapter is a miracle, but everything in it is the outworking of moral order. The chapter teaches that God's justice is built into the way the world works, so that plans of cruelty carry their own undoing.

He keeps His word. God had said to Abraham that whoever cursed his family would be cursed, Genesis 12:3, and that Amalek's memory would be blotted out, Exodus 17:14. Haman the Agagite is undone on both counts, and the text gives no explanation for it other than the character of the God who has spoken. Isaiah says of such moments, 'No weapon formed against you shall prosper', Isaiah 54:17, and Esther 7 is a picture of that verse in a Persian dining room.

He is patient and precise. It took years from Mordecai's good deed to the day it mattered, and it took a series of small events to bring Haman to the table. God does not hurry, and He is never late. A few chapters ago the sentence of death seemed final, and in one evening it is reversed. Scripture holds that the LORD is 'slow to anger', Exodus 34:6, and also that He does not leave the guilty unpunished, Exodus 34:7. Both are in this story: the time given to Haman to repent, and the day when the account is called in.

He is also the God who takes no delight in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 33:11. The story records the justice and not the joy, and the same Bible urges believers not to gloat, Proverbs 24:17. The God of Esther 7 is the God who will finally pray, in His Son, 'Father, forgive them', Luke 23:34, for those who wronged Him. The severity and the kindness are not opposed.

For worship, the chapter gives a reason for confidence. The people of God may be threatened but they cannot be abandoned, and the powers set against them will not last. It gives believers freedom to leave vengeance to God, Romans 12:19, and to keep speaking the truth when asked, as Esther did.

crossReferences.note: Haman offers silver and issues a decree to destroy, kill and annihilate all the Jews. Esther 7:4 quotes the same three verbs back to the king. Set side by side, the two chapters show how the plan is exposed by its own words.

Vashti refuses the king's summons, and his anger burns within him. The king's fury in 7:7 is the second time his rage falls on someone at a banquet, and the parallel shows how the book uses one emotion to frame both the fall of a queen and the fall of a minister.

The king's anger subsides after Vashti's removal, and he remembers what she did. Esther 7:10 uses the same phrase of the fury that subsides after Haman's death, and the echo closes the frame that chapter 1 began.

The wicked man digs a pit and falls into it, and his violence lands on his own head. The gallows in Esther 7:10 is the story's picture of the psalm, and the psalm supplies the moral explanation for what the narrator leaves unsaid.

The nations fall into the pit they made, and the wicked are ensnared by the work of their hands. The LORD is known by the justice He brings. The psalm names what Esther 7 shows, that the justice of God is visible in how evil returns on itself.

The righteous man is delivered from trouble, and the wicked man takes his place. The proverb could serve as a caption for the exchange of Mordecai and Haman, since the trouble prepared for the one is taken by the other.

Saul spares Agag, king of the Amalekites, and the best of the spoil, and leaves the task unfinished. Haman the Agagite is the outcome of that half-obedience, and Esther 7 shows the LORD finishing what Saul did not.

No accusation can stand against God's elect, since it is God who justifies and Christ who intercedes. The verses give the gospel's answer to the courtroom of Esther 7, where an accuser is silenced before a throne.

The accuser of the brothers is thrown down, and the saints overcome him by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony. It is the great counterpart of Haman's fall, and it names the true source of the enmity that the book of Esther only names as adversary.

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, since it is written that everyone hung on a tree is cursed. Haman hung on the wood for his own guilt, and Christ on the tree for ours.

study.oneStory:
Esther 7 is the moment when the Bible's long conflict between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent reaches one of its sharpest points before the coming of Christ. The conflict opens at Genesis 3:15, where God announces enmity and the eventual crushing of the serpent's head. From that verse, the story is full of attempts to destroy the line: Cain kills Abel, Pharaoh drowns the Hebrew boys, Amalek strikes the stragglers, and Haman decrees the death of the entire people. Each attempt seems to threaten the promise itself, and each fails.

The chapter answers a question that arises in exile. If God's people are scattered among the nations and subject to a foreign king's law, can the promises still hold? The Persian law could not be revoked, Esther 8:8, and the decree was as final as a law could be. This chapter shows that the enemy who wrote the decree cannot survive it. The story does not yet resolve the decree, which will be answered in chapter 8, but it removes the man behind it and shows that no earthly power is beyond the reach of the God who keeps His word to Abraham, Genesis 12:3.

The chapter also completes a thread that began in 1 Samuel 15. Saul's failure to finish Amalek left the enemy in the land, and the descendant of Agag rises to threaten the descendants of the man who spared him. It is one of the book's subtle strokes that the answer is given not through Saul's line by force, but by a Benjamite in exile who bows to no one but God, Esther 3:2 and 2:5. God's purposes outlast human failures.

Looking forward, the chapter is a preview of the cross. There, the accuser and his powers thought they had won, and at the cross they were disarmed, Colossians 2:15. Paul takes the curse of the tree and shows that Christ bore it, Galatians 3:13. The pattern of Haman's gallows is filled with a new meaning: the wood that was meant to condemn becomes the place where condemnation is removed.

The story ends in the new creation, where the great accuser is thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10, and God's people are safe forever, with 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain', Revelation 21:4. The narrow relief of Susa, where a people were rescued from one day of massacre, is a small sign of that final rescue, when no decree, no accuser and no death will threaten the redeemed.

sermon.title: Haman Is Hanged!
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Esther, this message expounds Esther 7:1-10, Esther's petition and the fall of Haman on his own gallows, tracing the unseen hand of God who works through a brave queen and a proud man's ruin to rescue His people. A faithful, expository handling of this movement.

quiz.q: What did Esther finally ask of the king at the second banquet?

options.text: That her own life and the lives of her people be spared from destruction.
options.note: Esther 7:3-4 shows her petition was for life, not treasure or rank.

options.text: That she be given half the kingdom as the king offered.
options.note: The king offered half the kingdom, but she asked only for life.

options.text: That Mordecai be promoted over Haman.
options.note: Her petition was the survival of her people, not a promotion for Mordecai.

options.text: That she be allowed to return to her homeland.
options.note: She asked for deliverance from death, not for return from exile.

quiz.q: How did the king come to see Haman as guilty of assaulting the queen?

options.text: He returned to find Haman fallen on Esther's couch as he begged for his life.
options.note: Esther 7:8 records the fatal misreading of Haman's desperate plea.

options.text: Esther accused Haman of attacking her directly.
options.note: The king drew the conclusion himself upon seeing Haman on the couch.

options.text: A servant testified that Haman had struck the queen.
options.note: No such testimony was given; the king judged by what he saw on returning.

options.text: Haman confessed to the crime.
options.note: Haman was pleading for his life, not confessing to any assault.

quiz.q: On what was Haman finally executed?

options.text: The very gallows he had built to hang Mordecai.
options.note: Esther 7:9-10 shows the plot recoiling exactly on the plotter.

options.text: A new gallows the king ordered constructed.
options.note: It was the gallows Haman himself had prepared for Mordecai.

options.text: The palace executioner's block.
options.note: He was hanged on his own gallows, the point of the irony.

options.text: A pyre in the city square.
options.note: The text specifies the gallows Haman raised for Mordecai.

quiz.q: What does Haman's death on his own gallows most clearly teach?

options.text: A hidden God turns the schemes of the wicked back upon their own heads.
options.note: The exact fit of punishment to crime reveals God's just governance.

options.text: That clever queens can outwit foolish kings.
options.note: Esther's courage matters, but the lesson is God's justice, not mere cleverness.

options.text: That anger is always a reliable guide to justice.
options.note: The king's rage served God's ends, but Scripture does not commend rage as a guide.

options.text: That God rescues only through visible miracles.
options.note: The opposite: here God works with no miracle at all, through ordinary events.

quiz.q: How does this chapter point forward to Christ?

options.text: The accuser is cast down and the condemned is spared, fulfilled when Christ disarmed the accuser at the cross.
options.note: Colossians 2:15 shows the true accuser overthrown on the tree of death.

options.text: Haman is a picture of the suffering Saviour.
options.note: Haman is the enemy cast down, not a picture of the Saviour.

options.text: The banquet foreshadows the Lord's Supper directly.
options.note: The setting is a banquet, but the christological point is the accuser's defeat.

options.text: The chapter has no bearing on the gospel.
options.note: The reversal of accuser and condemned runs straight to the cross.

questions: Esther waited for the right moment, then spoke the truth even at great risk to herself. Where is God calling you to speak up for others, even when it may cost you?
Haman was destroyed by the very trap he built for someone else. Where might the schemes or resentments you are nursing against another person actually be a pit you are digging for yourself?
The king's fury, an ordinary human temper, became the means of rescue. How does it change your view of God's providence to see Him work even through the moods and tempers of powerful people?
The one marked for the gallows was spared, and the accuser was cast down. How does the assurance that no charge can stand against you in Christ steady you when you feel condemned?
God is never named in this chapter, yet His justice is unmistakable. Where in your own life are you being invited to trust that God is at work even when He seems hidden?

translationNotes.note: The narrator's aside about the one who would devise such a scheme renders a vivid Hebrew idiom, literally whose heart has filled him to do this; the sense is the same, the man bold enough to plot it.
Fifty cubits is roughly seventy-five feet or twenty-three meters; the towering height underscores Haman's arrogance and the public spectacle of his fall.
